title: CFA Alternatives 7: Digital assets seen through the alternatives framework
subtitle: Classifying by function, the custody mechanism, and why 'uncorrelated' is a claim that needs testing
whyItMatters: CFA Institute has made digital assets a Learning Module of their own, and their approach differs sharply from the usual debates: it does not ask whether crypto has value, but which category it belongs to and which risks it carries that other assets do not.
openingQuestion: In the CFA curriculum's taxonomy, on what basis are digital assets classified?
openingOptions: By market capitalisation, from largest to smallest
By the economic function each type of token performs
By the underlying technology each one is built on
By how far regulators in each country have accepted them
explanation: Classifying by function is what makes the framework usable. A coin used for payment, a token granting the right to use a service on a platform, a token representing ownership of a real asset, and a coin pegged to fiat currency - these four have entirely different sources of value, legal treatment and risks, even though they run on similar technology. In many countries a security token falls under exactly the same securities law as a share. For a stablecoin, the main risk is not technological at all but the quality of the reserve assets behind it - precisely the risk profile of a money market fund.

summary.keyIdea: The biggest risk in this asset class is not price volatility but custody: lose the key and the asset is gone permanently, a form of operational risk traditional assets do not have.
summary.commonMistake: Treating the whole group as a single asset type. A reserve-backed stablecoin and a utility token share no meaningful risk at all.

application.title: The risk that rarely gets mentioned
application.message: Custody risk. Losing the key means losing the asset, with no recovery mechanism anywhere - a form of operational risk that does not exist in traditional assets.

sections.text: Digital assets are not a homogeneous group. Classifying them by function - rather than by technology - is what turns the analytical framework into something you can actually use.

items: Payment coins: value comes from how widely they are accepted and how credible the scarcity commitment is.
Utility tokens: grant the right to use a service on a platform, so value is tied to genuine demand for that platform.
Security tokens: represent ownership of a real asset, and in many countries fall squarely under securities law.
Stablecoins: pegged to fiat currency, with value depending on the quality of the reserve assets behind them.

sections.label: The most important point
sections.text: These four groups have entirely different sources of value, legal frameworks and risks, even though they run on similar technology. A stablecoin should be analysed as a money market fund, not as a technology asset.
Custody risk - a form of risk traditional assets do not have

With equities, losing access to your account does not lose you the asset: there is a share register, a central depository and a recovery process. With a digital asset held directly, losing the private key is permanent, and leaving it on an exchange means taking on that exchange's credit risk. This is why most institutional investors only participate through a licensed custodian.

sections.label: Careful with the correlation figure
sections.text: The widely quoted 'uncorrelated' claim is an estimate from a short slice of history, and recent stress episodes show correlation rising at exactly the moment you needed it to stay low.

lines: Shared technology does not mean shared risk.
Ask what right this token gives you, and only then ask what it is worth.

diagram.label: Payment coin: value from widespread acceptance
Utility token: the right to use a platform service
Security token: ownership, and securities law with it
Stablecoin: the risk sits in the reserve assets behind it

realWorldExample.company: Custody risk - a risk traditional assets do not carry
realWorldExample.description: With equities, losing your paperwork does not lose you ownership, because a central register holds it. With a digital asset held directly, losing the private key is permanent and nobody can restore it. Leaving it with an exchange swaps that risk for counterparty risk - and several large collapses have shown how real that one is. This is a category of operational risk the traditional analytical framework has nowhere to put, which is why it tends to be dropped when expected returns are compared.

quiz.question: Why is classifying digital assets by function more useful than by market capitalisation?
options: Because market capitalisation in digital assets moves so fast
Because the four functions differ in source of value and risk
Because regulators now demand assets be classified by function
Because market cap fails to reflect genuine trading volume
quiz.explanation: A classification is only useful when the groups genuinely require different analysis - and here they do. Market capitalisation ranks tokens without telling you what any of them is; two assets of identical size can be a claim on a pool of reserves and a licence to use a piece of software. No regulator prescribes this taxonomy, and the volume objection, while true, is a data-quality complaint rather than a reason to classify by function.

quiz.question: Where does the main risk of a stablecoin sit?
options: In how sharply its price swings with the wider crypto market
In the transaction throughput of the underlying network
In the quality and liquidity of the reserves behind it
In how many users accept it as a means of payment
quiz.explanation: This is money market fund risk rather than technology risk - and it is analysed with exactly those tools: what sits in the reserve, how quickly it can be sold, and who is holding it. A stablecoin holds its peg because redemptions can be met, not because the network is fast; throughput and adoption matter to a payment token, not to whether a peg survives.

quiz.question: How does custody risk for a digital asset differ from that of an equity?
options: Digital assets must be held at a licensed custodian institution
Lose the private key and it is gone; no register can restore it
Equities carry more custody risk, being held via a brokerage firm
There is no difference; both rest on a central register of owners
quiz.explanation: This is a class of operational risk the traditional framework has no place for, so it tends to get dropped when returns are compared. Nothing obliges an individual to use a licensed custodian - self-custody is the default position. Equities sit on a central register that survives the loss of any document or password, which is exactly the safety net a private key does not have.

quiz.question: What legally separates a security token from a utility token?
options: In many countries a security token falls under securities law
Utility tokens are banned from issuance across most jurisdictions
Security tokens may not be traded on any secondary market
Both sit entirely outside the scope of the law as it stands
quiz.explanation: Economic substance determines the legal framework, not the name or the technology - this is a general principle of securities regulation, and it is why calling something a utility token does not make it one. Utility tokens are not banned in most places, security tokens do trade on regulated secondary venues, and the claim that both fall outside the law describes an era that has largely passed.

quiz.question: How should the claim that 'crypto is uncorrelated with equities' be handled?
options: Accept it, since the two rest on completely different mechanisms
Test it, because correlation shifts and tends to rise under stress
Reject it, because every risky asset is perfectly correlated
Ignore it, because correlation is not a factor in allocation
quiz.explanation: Correlation is an estimate drawn from one particular window of data, not a fixed property of an asset - and it has a habit of rising exactly when you need it low. Different underlying mechanisms do not settle it, because in a liquidity squeeze investors sell what they can rather than what is related. And nothing is perfectly correlated either; that overstates the case as badly as the original claim did.

keyTakeaways: Classify by function: payment, utility, security, stablecoin
Stablecoins: the risk sits in the reserves, so analyse them as a money market fund
Security tokens fall under securities law because of economic substance, not the name
Custody risk is a form of risk traditional assets do not carry
'Uncorrelated' is an estimate from one window, and correlation rises when markets are stressed

practicePrompt.question: A fund proposes allocating 5% of a pension portfolio to digital assets on the grounds that it 'improves diversification'. What is the first question to ask?
options: What expected return is being assumed for digital assets over the next five years
Which period the correlation estimate comes from, and how it behaved in stress episodes
Which specific digital currencies the fund is intending to buy for the mandate
What transaction costs and management fees apply to this part of the allocation
practicePrompt.explanation: The diversification argument rests entirely on a correlation estimate, so that is where the checking has to start. The other three questions are all reasonable, but they come afterwards: if correlation jumps at precisely the moment the portfolio needed protecting, no expected return and no fee level can rescue the original argument.
